name: Emotional reasoning
statement: Anxious people read their own anxiety as evidence that a situation is dangerous, so the feeling of threat becomes a reason to believe in the threat.
meaning: The claim is about the direction of an inference. Fear normally follows danger, and the reasoning under test runs the other way, from the feeling back to the world. Arntz, Rauner and van den Hout called it ex-consequentia reasoning, inferring the premise from the consequence. Its clinical interest is the loop it implies. Anxiety indicates threat, the inferred threat sustains the anxiety, and the person never finds out that the situation was safe. The task built to test it separates two sources of information, what a scene objectively contains and what the person feels, then asks which one the danger rating follows.

origin.who: Arnoud Arntz, Michael Rauner and Marcel van den Hout
origin.note: The abstract opens by saying the idea had already been suggested, that neurotic patients draw invalid conclusions from their own emotional response. Gangemi, Dahò and Mancini trace the description to Beck, Emery and Greenberg's 1985 book on anxiety disorders and quote it from page 198; that book was not read here.

evidence: The 1995 experiment gave people short scripts and asked how dangerous the situation was. Each script crossed two factors: objective safety against objective danger, and an anxious response against a calm one. Gangemi and colleagues quote the panic script from page 919. The reader is in a crowded lift, and the ending either has a passenger falling into their arms as a welcome chance, or has the lift stuck between floors with two people fainting, each version running with or without the line that the reader suddenly becomes anxious. A danger rating that rises with the anxious ending counts as emotional reasoning. The abstract reports 52 spider phobics, 41 panic patients, 38 social phobics, 31 other anxiety patients and 24 normal controls. Patients' ratings followed the anxiety information as well as the objective information, and the controls' ratings followed the objective information alone. The abstract adds that the effect was neither situation-specific nor confined to panic patients, so patients did it on scripts unrelated to their own diagnosis.

replication.headline: The danger-inflating effect turns up again in anxious and fearful samples, and the result that separated patients from everybody else does not.
replication.detail: Engelhard, Macklin, McNally, van den Hout and Arntz gave the scenarios to Vietnam combat veterans. Veterans without PTSD inferred danger from the objective information, while veterans with PTSD also inferred it from anxiety and from intrusive memories, and both effects were largely mediated by perceived uncontrollability. The 2022 systematic review records this as the one included study that used Arntz's scenarios without modification. Verwoerd and colleagues ran the design twice with disgust in place of anxiety, comparing 31 people above the clinical range on contamination fear with 27 below it, and 35 people high on a measure of fear of vomiting with 38 low. High scorers in both studies inferred risk of illness from their disgust. The control-group result is the part that has not held. Muris, Merckelbach and van Spauwen found a general emotional reasoning effect in 101 primary school children, with anxiety sensitivity and trait anxiety predicting how far a child leaned on anxiety information in the safety scripts. Morren, Muris and Kindt found the effect in 508 children aged 7 to 13, and Morren and colleagues found it on two occasions ten months apart in 122 non-clinical children. Berle and Moulds gave an adapted task to 70 students split into 28 low and 42 high dysphoric on the Beck Depression Inventory. Both groups showed emotional reasoning, the groups did not differ, and they did not differ on the panic item carried over from Arntz either.

study.cite: Engelhard, I. M., Macklin, M. L., McNally, R. J., van den Hout, M. A., & Arntz, A. (2001). Emotion- and intrusion-based reasoning in Vietnam veterans with and without chronic posttraumatic stress disorder. Behaviour Research and Therapy, 39(11), 1339-1348.

limits: The evidence base is small and comes from one tradition. The 2022 systematic review searched PubMed, PsycInfo, Scopus and The Cochrane Library and included nine articles, the earliest from 1995 and the latest from 2016. Five were run in the Netherlands, three in Australia and one in Italy. Seven were case-control studies scoring 7 to 9 out of 12 on the review's quality tool, and one of the nine justified its sample size. No meta-analysis, multi-site replication or preregistered replication of the 1995 experiment turned up in the searches run for this entry, which covered Europe PMC, Crossref, and the reference lists of the 2022 review and of Gangemi, Dahò and Mancini. Every study rates imagined scenarios rather than felt emotion, a limitation Verwoerd and colleagues state about their own work. The 1995 paper is paywalled and only its abstract was read here. That matters, because the review's table describes the study as 133 people including 9 spider phobics, while the abstract gives 52 spider phobics among 162 patients. Gangemi and colleagues refer to a first experiment, so the paper may report more than one, and this entry cannot settle the discrepancy.
misreadings: The finding is often read as a line between anxious people and everybody else. Non-clinical children show the effect whatever their anxiety level, and dysphoric and non-dysphoric students showed it alike, so symptoms track the size of the tendency rather than its presence. The name also invites confusion with the affect heuristic, which comes from the judgement-and-decision-making literature and is tested against risk and benefit ratings and against probability weighting. Both describe a feeling standing in for evidence, and their evidence bases do not meet. Nothing resembling the Many Labs 2 test that broke one affect heuristic prediction has been run on Arntz's task. The depression case is also not the anxiety case. Berle and Moulds found no difference between currently depressed and non-depressed participants across 78 people, and the 2022 review reports no group differences for depressive symptoms in either of the two studies that looked.
